title: ViroGym: Realistic Large-Scale Benchmarks for Evaluating Viral Proteins
claim: A benchmark unifies model training, scoring strategies, in-vitro assays and real-world forecasting tasks, with shared metrics, in one evaluation framework.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right; vertical model pipeline feeding two task panels
description: A three-part diagram. The left column is a vertical flow. A dashed ellipse holds training databases (UniProtKB, OAS, BFD). An arrow labelled 'Train' leads to a grey 'Pre-trained Protein Language Models' box with a neural-net icon. An arrow labelled 'Evaluate' leads to a dashed box, 'Fitness Scoring Strategies', which lists masked marginals, wild-type marginals, mutation marginals, pseudo-likelihood and perplexity. An arrow from this box points right into the task area. The middle panel, 'In-Vitro Experiments', shows a stacked red-yellow-green DMS heatmap (amino acid vs residue) above a neutralisation-assay scatter plot (titer vs serum, virus A and B). The right panel, 'Real World Tasks', shows a pandemic-forecasting heatmap above a dashed 'Metrics' box with a histogram icon and the bullets Spearman correlation, Top K% recall and Precision@K. 'ViroGym' appears in the bottom-right corner.
caption: ViroGym benchmark framework. The benchmark comprises in vitro experimental evaluation and real-world prediction tasks. The in vitro component uses DMS and neutralisation measurements to evaluate model predictions of protein functional effects. The real-world component evaluates SARS-CoV-2 pandemic forecasting using GISAID sequences, assessing generalisation from controlled wet-lab settings to natural viral evolution.
abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) have shown strong potential for zero-shot prediction of missense variant effects, yet systematic benchmarking on viral proteins remains limited, a critical gap given the need for proactive tools that can anticipate emerging mutations ahead of experimental validation. Here we introduce ViroGym, a comprehensive benchmark evaluating pLMs across three tasks: 79 deep mutational scanning (DMS) assays covering eukaryotic viruses with 552,065 mutated sequences across 7 phenotypic readouts, 21 influenza neutralisation tasks, and a real-world pandemic prediction task for SARS-CoV-2. We benchmark well-established pLMs on fitness landscapes, antigenic diversity, and pandemic forecasting, and find that the ProGen2 family consistently achieves the strongest performance across all three tasks. Crucially, DMS and neutralisation performance reliably identifies models that generalise to real-world emergence, even though the mutation sets they surface barely overlap, revealing that complementary in vitro benchmarks capture the evolutionary constraints needed for real-world mutation forecasting. The data and code supporting this study are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/GSK-AI/viroGym
